description: We are team from National Physics Mathematics School
summary:
We developed BLFA (Beyond LEO Fire Audit), an interactive, SI-powered fire safety dashboard and deterministic cabin-toxicity simulator (blfa-deploy.vercel.app) built for NASA's Flame in Freefall challenge.

To make decades of fragmented microgravity combustion research—including BASS, SAME, SoFIE-MIST, and Saffire—actionable for mission planners, BLFA audits six foundational International Space Station (ISS) firefighting assumptions against five deep-space exploration vehicles: Orion, Lunar Lander, Pressurized Rover, Lunar Surface Habitat, and Mars Transit. Using an interactive 6x5 Doctrine x Vehicle Matrix paired with a physics-based gas-mixing and suppression engine calibrated to NASA-STD-3001 and NASA-STD-6001B, the platform summarizes, ranks, and classifies each rule as Holds, Degrades, Breaks, or Unknown.

This tool is critical because firefighting rules designed for a 900 m3, zero-gravity ISS fail dangerously beyond Low Earth Orbit. In partial lunar (0.16g) and Martian (0.38g) gravity, natural buoyancy returns to feed flames even when fans are shut off, while tiny 9-20 m3 cabins concentrate CO2 extinguishers, exhaled oxygen masks, and post-fire toxic gases to lethal levels within seconds. BLFA identifies which ISS procedures must be rewritten before Artemis and Mars missions launch.
details:
What It Does & How It Works BLFA (Beyond LEO Fire Audit) is an interactive, Super Intelligence (SI) powered fire safety dashboard and deterministic gas-mixing simulation engine built for NASA's Flame in Freefall challenge (deployed at blfa-deploy.vercel.app). Decades of microgravity combustion data—spanning NASA payloads such as BASS, SAME, SoFIE-MIST, and Saffire—are scattered across isolated technical papers and raw Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) datasets. BLFA synthesizes this evidence into a 6x5 Doctrine-by-Vehicle Audit Matrix that evaluates six foundational International Space Station (ISS) firefighting assumptions against five deep-space exploration vehicles: Orion MPCV, Lunar Lander, Pressurized Rover, Lunar Surface Habitat, and Mars Transit Habitat. Each intersection is algorithmically graded into one of four engineering states—Holds, Degrades, Breaks, or Unknown—backed by experimental citations and a real-time cabin toxicity simulator calibrated against NASA-STD-3001 human survival limits and NASA-STD-6001B flammability standards.

Benefits & Intended Impact Instead of forcing mission planners and safety engineers to manually cross-reference hundreds of pages of microgravity combustion literature, BLFA summarizes, ranks, and translates complex experimental physics into immediate operational decisions. Its primary impact is preventing fatal firefighting errors during Artemis and Mars missions. By explicitly exposing where ISS rules fail—and highlighting Unknown data blind spots where no long-duration partial-gravity testing exists—BLFA gives NASA a prioritized roadmap for rewriting emergency crew procedures, redesigning small-cabin extinguishers and breathing masks, and selecting future lunar combustion payloads.

Tools, Coding Languages & Software Used

  • Simulation and Backend Logic: Python (leveraging NumPy and Pandas) for deterministic cabin gas-mixing, CO2 suppression, oxygen enrichment, and post-fire toxicity calculations alongside custom data structures.
  • Frontend and Deployment: Modern web stack (HTML, CSS, JavaScript/React) engineered with a high-contrast, utilitarian, data-dense brutalist UI architecture and hosted in production on Vercel (blfa-deploy.vercel.app).
  • Data and Standards Sources: NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) microgravity combustion datasets (BASS, SAME, SoFIE-MIST, Saffire), NASA Glenn Research Center partial-gravity updates, NASA-STD-3001, NASA-STD-6001B, and Spacecraft Maximum Allowable Concentrations (SMAC).

What Makes It Creative Most combustion tools treat space fire data as passive literature search or isolated flame visualizations. BLFA reframes the entire problem as a doctrinal stress test—auditing human emergency playbooks rather than just burning materials. Pairing an executive 6x5 failure matrix with a deterministic physics engine that simulates exact cabin volume and gravity shifts turns historical ISS data into a predictive survival tool. Furthermore, treating missing data (Unknown) as a first-class analytical output turns gaps in NASA's historical record into actionable research recommendations.

Key Factors Our Team Considered

  • Gravity Transitions (0g vs. 0.16g and 0.38g): On the 0g ISS, cutting ventilation fans suffocates flames due to the absence of buoyancy; under lunar (0.16g) and Martian (0.38g) gravity, natural upward convection returns and continuously feeds oxygen to fires even with fans turned off.
  • Cabin Volume Scaling (900 m3 vs. 9 to 20 m3): Small vehicles like Orion and the Pressurized Rover concentrate CO2 extinguisher discharges, exhaled oxygen from open-vent masks, and toxic combustion byproducts (CO, HF, HCl, HCN) 40 to 100 times faster than the ISS.
  • Exploration Atmospheres (21% O2 vs. 34% O2): Lunar and Martian habitats plan to operate at reduced pressure (8.2 psi) and elevated oxygen (34% O2) to streamline spacewalks, while SoFIE-MIST and centrifuge tests show the Limiting Oxygen Concentration drops from roughly 18% on Earth to roughly 15% in orbit and lunar gravity.
  • Sensor Blind Spots and Zero-Escape Constraints: SAME data proved ISS optical smoke detectors miss burning Kapton 50% of the time and Teflon 67% of the time. Combined with multi-day or multi-month return times where crew evacuation is impossible, post-fire air scrubbing and early detection outweigh thermal heat as the primary survival bottleneck.
